bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is the product-level design work that makes alarms, warnings, alerts, fault states, mute states, and recovery signals understandable under real operating conditions. Alarm management as a discipline, including lifecycle models, standards regimes, and common failure modes, is addressed separately on the Alarm Management page. This page describes what Creative Navy does inside specific products when alarm clarity is part of the design problem.

Creative Navy's documented warning and alarm work covers regulated medical alarm architecture, redundant cue design in surgical devices, fault prioritisation in multi-engine marine displays, consumer alert tiering, silent failure surfacing in simulation software, embedded vehicle warning redesign, and industrial alarm rationalisation.

## When warning and alarm clarity is needed

Warning and alarm clarity is needed when a product can signal a condition that users must notice, interpret, prioritise, and act on. The design problem is not only whether an alarm appears. The design problem is whether the alarm directs attention to the right condition, communicates urgency, gives the user a next action when action is required, and remains visible enough that it cannot be forgotten.

Alert fatigue, also called alarm fatigue, occurs when users encounter too many alarms or too many low-priority alarms. False positives and nuisance alarms are identified in the documented evidence as primary drivers of alert fatigue. In process-industry settings, the repeat-alarm rate is used as a measure of nuisance-alarm burden.

Actionability is a separate requirement from visibility. An actionable warning communicates both what is wrong and what to do. In time-pressured environments, a warning that communicates a problem without a next action is not actionable.

Redundant cues are required when operating conditions can degrade any single communication channel. Variable lighting, noise, vibration, divided attention, gloves, night-vision constraints, or theatre lighting can make a single cue unreliable. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, warning states were therefore communicated through spatial position, icon form, and colour at the same time.

## What Creative Navy designs in warning and alarm clarity work

Creative Navy's warning and alarm clarity work defines the structural rules that govern how warnings, overlays, alarm layers, and interruptive elements relate to the product interface. This is warning architecture: the structural logic that must be established before individual warning components are designed.

The capability includes priority tiering, where alarm states are ranked by urgency and made visually distinguishable. In the Kardion MCS Controller case, priority levels were tied to clinical urgency and had to be unambiguously distinguishable under IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements.

The capability includes visual differentiation beyond colour. In the Kardion MCS Controller case, each priority level used a distinct combination of colour, icon, border treatment, and spatial behaviour. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, benchmarking found that most of the 6 comparable devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions; the redesign used three independent cue channels.

The capability includes mute behaviour. A muted alarm must remain visually present at reduced prominence and must not be dismissible into a state where an active alarm is invisible.

The capability includes recovery indication. A recovery indication tells users that a previously alarmed condition has resolved. Without a recovery indication, users cannot confirm whether their action was effective.

The capability includes silent failure warnings. In expert software, a process can complete normally while producing output that appears valid but is structurally incorrect. In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, warning design had to interrupt this form of silent failure before or after simulation runs.

## Kardion MCS Controller: regulated alarm architecture under IEC 60601-1-8 and IEC 62366-1

The Kardion MCS Controller case is the most formal documented alarm-architecture example. The alarm architecture was not treated as a design preference. The requirements were derived from use-related hazards identified through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process, while the alarm-system requirements were set by IEC 60601-1-8 for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment.

Creative Navy's design work for Kardion included priority tiering, visual differentiation beyond colour, mute behaviour, and explicit alarm state visibility. The absence of an alarm had to be confirmable as a system state; operators needed to confirm that no active alarms existed, rather than merely observe the absence of an alarm indicator.

The Kardion alarm requirements constrained the standard view by reserving some spatial positions and visual treatments for the alarm layer. That removed those options from the nominal state hierarchy and clarified the remaining option space for the interface.

The regulatory result is recorded as FDA approval: the design passed evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. The alarm architecture contributed to the review satisfying identified use-related hazards related to alarm misinterpretation and missed alarms. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## deSoutter Medical / Zethon: redundant cues for warning recognition under theatre lighting

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon case shows alarm-channel design under variable operating conditions. Benchmarking found that most of the 6 benchmarked comparable devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions. Under variable theatre lighting, including repositioned surgical headlights and adjusted overhead illumination, colour coding becomes unreliable.

Creative Navy's design response used three independent communication channels for every critical state and warning: spatial position, icon form, and colour. Spatial position made the indicator readable when colour and icon form were unclear. Icon form carried meaning independently of colour. Colour remained present but was no longer the only cue.

The design decision was governed by IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation and directly addressed the use-related hazard of state misinterpretation under operating theatre conditions. Surgeon feedback from design review sessions reported that state verification was reduced to brief glance recognition. That statement is design review session feedback, not post-deployment measurement.

## Cox Marine cluster displays: fault prioritisation in multi-engine configurations

The Cox Marine cluster displays case addresses a fault-prioritisation problem in multi-engine configurations. When several engines are present, an alarm must direct attention to the priority engine, not merely signal that a fault exists somewhere.

Creative Navy identified the issue during scenario testing in Concept Convergence. Designs that passed nominal-state evaluation failed the multi-engine fault scenario because they surfaced fault presence without directing attention. A design that requires captains to scan 6 tiles for a fault source under time pressure is treated as a design failure even if the fault indicator is technically visible.

The resulting two-level alarm architecture used a dedicated fault-summary area to surface the highest-priority condition across all engine tiles, followed by per-tile alarm highlighting so captains could confirm the source. A military night vision mode added a hard constraint: all alarm states, including the two-level structure, had to remain distinguishable under night vision goggles. That constraint eliminated several colour and contrast approaches that would otherwise have been viable.

## Elsner Elektronik: alert tiering for a non-technical consumer audience

The Elsner Elektronik case shows why alarm wording and priority must match the user's ability to act. The consumer embedded-device audience included non-technical occupants who could not address sensor faults directly. A technical fault code presented to someone who cannot interpret it is not an effective alarm; it becomes noise that trains users to ignore later alarms.

Creative Navy's design response used a dual-priority alert system. General alerts covered routine conditions such as a sensor outside the preferred range, calibration drift, or delayed readings. They used low-urgency visual and auditory signalling and communicated that something could be adjusted or that an engineer should be informed when convenient.

Critical notifications covered complete sensor failure and safety-relevant state changes. They used distinct visual treatment and escalated auditory signalling to communicate that something required immediate attention. The distinction was calibrated to the audience: general alert meant something to know about; critical notification meant something to act on now.

## Gexcon CFD simulation: warnings for silent failure in expert software

The Gexcon CFD simulation case addresses silent failure in expert software. The error did not stop the system. The simulation could complete normally and produce output that appeared valid, while the configuration was structurally incorrect.

Before redesign, available case evidence records 5–8 configuration errors per simulation, each requiring 4–6 hours of corrective work. The warning architecture addressed the problem at three points in the workflow: during scenario setup, at contradictory inputs, and at post-run error detection.

During scenario setup, warnings surfaced incomplete required values before the simulation ran. At contradictory inputs, warnings surfaced internally contradictory values before the simulation was initiated. At post-run error detection, warnings specified the error, its location in the configuration, and the corrective action.

Each warning was designed against an actionability standard: the user had to understand both what was wrong and what to do. The documented outcome was a reduction in configuration errors from 5–8 to 1–2, and a reduction in corrective load from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes. The warning architecture is identified in the case evidence as a primary mechanism for both reductions.

## Stromer e-bike embedded display: warning architecture after overlay failure

The Stromer e-bike embedded display case shows why warning architecture must be defined before warning components. A previous external agency had designed the screen architecture first and then added warnings as overlays. The warnings had no native relationship to the surface they were placed on.

The consequences were observable and classifiable. Warnings covered screen content they should not cover. Warnings interfered with active interactions. Some warnings were too persistent, while others were too easily dismissed. Some warnings appeared without enough context for riders to understand what they referred to.

The product carried safety warnings, status alerts, error states, and threshold notifications. EN 15194:2017 specified requirements for warning device symbology and behaviour. Regulatory colour conventions constrained some decisions, including a tire pressure sensor workstream where yellow was specified for sensor malfunction states while severity logic called for red.

Creative Navy redesigned the layout and overlay system, the information architecture, and the rules governing how warnings and interruptive elements relate to the screen structure. The evaluation was Creative Navy-designed and run: 10 participants rode the bike for 3 days each on real routes in Munich and surrounding countryside, logging every issue by severity on a 4-level scale.

Before the redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention. After the redesign, the same test used 10 users, including 6 returning users and 4 replacements, with the same bikes, routes, and logging protocol. Warnings did not appear on the issues list. Creative Navy ran the same test again two years later, and warnings remained absent.

Eye tracking in actual riding conditions with 5 participants on the same routes recorded a reduction in average glance duration at the display from 4.32 seconds to 1.89 seconds. The result moved average glance duration from more than twice the 2-second threshold established by road safety research cited as Klauer et al. (2006) and NHTSA Driver Distraction Guidelines Phase 1 to within the safe zone. Glance frequency per kilometre fell by 18%.

## Gericke industrial HMI: alarm rationalisation and root-cause hierarchy

The Gericke industrial HMI case is the documented industrial alarm-management example. The relevant alarm-management frameworks were ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682. Gericke operated in GMP environments, with GAMP 5 relevant; it was not a regulated device and was not governed by IEC 62366-1.

The legacy interface showed two central failure modes together. It had no priority hierarchy: operator testing found operators attending to the most visible alarm rather than the most relevant alarm. It also produced alarm flooding, where a single fault generated a cascade of secondary alarms handled symptom by symptom. Alarms were raw error codes with no corrective path, requiring manual lookup.

Creative Navy's design response combined alarm rationalisation with a root-cause hierarchy. Secondary alarms were collapsed beneath their originating event, and probable cause was indicated so operators could address the cause rather than chase effects. A conveying-blockage reconstruction highlighted “Valve V12 failed to reach open position — probable root cause of 6 active alarms” directly on the process path.

Contextual alarm explanations replaced raw codes with plain explanations of the condition and what to do. The documented redesign also included the case where the correct action was no action: a refill-cycle event was surfaced as “temporary deviation expected — no operator action required,” with secondary alarms grouped beneath it.

The measured alarm-quality outcome was repeat-alarm rate, the process-industry measure of nuisance-alarm burden. Results were client-measured by Gericke at three sites within a confirmed single-variable window: 42% to 18% at a Swiss pharma site, 58% to 28% at an Italian food site, and 73% to 35% at a Swiss chemicals site. Fault-diagnosis time fell over the same period from 24 to 8 minutes, 38 to 12 minutes, and 68 to 20 minutes.

## Evidence basis for warning and alarm clarity improvement

The evidence for this capability is case-based and varies by engagement. The Kardion MCS Controller case provides regulated alarm-architecture evidence under IEC 60601-1-8 and IEC 62366-1, including FDA approval wording and a formative-only scope caveat.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon case provides design-review and formative-evaluation evidence for redundant cues under operating theatre conditions. The surgeon-reported glance recognition finding is feedback from design review sessions, not post-deployment measurement.

The Cox Marine cluster displays case provides scenario-testing evidence from Concept Convergence for multi-engine fault prioritisation and night vision constraints.

The Elsner Elektronik case provides a consumer embedded-device example of alert tiering for non-technical users.

The Gexcon CFD simulation case provides measured before-and-after reductions in configuration errors and corrective load, with warning architecture identified as a primary mechanism.

The Stromer e-bike embedded display case provides Creative Navy-designed and run field testing across three rounds and Creative Navy-measured eye tracking in actual riding conditions.

The Gericke industrial HMI case provides client-measured process-industry outcomes at three sites, including repeat-alarm rate and fault-diagnosis time. The “most visible versus most relevant” finding came from operator testing. The conveying-blockage and refill-cycle examples are Creative Navy reconstructions of the redesign, not logged incidents.

## Boundaries and limits

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is not the same as the full alarm-management discipline. Alarm management includes lifecycle, standards regimes, and process governance; this capability addresses how Creative Navy designs alarm clarity in specific product interfaces.

Regulated medical-device alarm work must keep formative design work separate from summative validation and regulatory submission. In the Kardion case, Creative Navy's role was formative only; summative validation and regulatory submission were the manufacturer's responsibility.

Not all evidence has the same strength. Stromer includes Creative Navy-designed and run field testing and Creative Navy-measured eye tracking. Gericke outcomes were client-measured by Gericke. DeSoutter surgeon feedback came from design review sessions. Gericke examples include reconstructions of the redesign rather than logged incidents.

Standards differ by context. IEC 60601-1-8 and IEC 62366-1 governed the Kardion alarm architecture. ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682 were relevant to Gericke's industrial alarm-management context. EN 15194:2017 constrained warning device symbology and behaviour in the Stromer e-bike workstream.

## Related pages

Alarm Management is the related discipline page for alarm lifecycle, standards regimes, and failure modes. Design For Abnormal And Degraded Scenarios is relevant where alarm states appear during fault, degraded, or high-pressure conditions. Error Reduction And Recovery Design is relevant where warnings must prevent or correct user errors. State And Status Visibility Design is relevant where alarms, recovery indications, and normal-state confirmation depend on visible system state.
